title: Half Shiva, half Shakti
hookLine: a devotee tries to honor Shiva without Parvati; why Hindus worship God as Ardhanarishvara, both halves at once
carry: shiva and shakti can't be split
tomorrow: the Goddess once came as a swarm of bees. why bees?
last: TIME BREATHES IN CYCLES, AND RESTS IN GOD.

lines: ONE BODY: HALF SHIVA, HALF PARVATI.
cards: Day one hundred, and a story about a devotee who went too far. Bhringi loved Shiva so much that he would walk circles around him in worship, the way people still walk around a shrine. Only Shiva.
Never Parvati, sitting right beside him. So she moved closer, until there was no gap. Bhringi tried to squeeze between them anyway.
And in the telling, Parvati did something remarkable: she merged into Shiva's body. Now there was one figure. The right half Shiva, the left half Parvati.
No gap left to slip through.

teach.h: ARDHANARISHVARA: THE LORD WHO IS HALF WOMAN.
teach.b: That form has a name: Ardhanarishvara, the Lord who is half woman. It's carved in temples across India, and has been for many centuries. Bhringi learned the hard way.

In many tellings, Parvati took back what a mother gives, his flesh and blood, and he couldn't stand, until Shiva, kind even then, gave him a third leg. Temples often show him beside Shiva, thin as bone, on three legs.
And here's the teaching, one of Hinduism's biggest: Shiva and Shakti. Shiva is often described as pure awareness, perfectly still. Shakti, the Goddess, is power, the energy that moves everything.
Many Hindus say you never have one without the other: Shiva without Shakti can't move, and power without awareness has nothing to stand on. To honor God is to honor both. Now the breath.
Nadi shodhana: nadi, a channel, and shodhana, clearing.
Yoga pictures two main channels: ida on the left, cool like the moon, and pingala on the right, warm like the sun, with sushumna in the center, along the spine.
Breathing side to side, the old teachers said, brings them into balance, and many teachers read yoga's aim as the two meeting in the middle, Shakti rising to meet Shiva. Here's how.
Right hand up, index and middle fingers folded. Thumb closes the right nostril; breathe in through the left.

teach.h: IN LEFT, OUT RIGHT, IN RIGHT, OUT LEFT.
teach.b: Ring finger closes the left, open the right; breathe out through the right.

teach.h: SHIVA AND SHAKTI CAN'T BE SPLIT.
teach.b: In through the right, switch, out through the left. Gentle, slow, no holding. If your nose is blocked, skip it and picture the breath moving side to side.

how: Ardhanarishvara, Shiva and Parvati as one figure, is worshipped and carved in temples across India. In yoga practice, nadi shodhana, alternate-nostril breathing using the thumb and ring finger of the right hand, is a common daily pranayama, often done before meditation or puja.

o: holding the breath to clean out the lungs
fast breathing through both sides to warm up
clearing the channels, one nostril at a time

games.q: a friend wants to pray to Shiva but says the Goddess part isn't really for him. what fits today's teaching?
o: in this picture there's no Shiva without Shakti: Ardhanarishvara holds both in one body.
that's fine: Parvati is an optional extra in Shiva's worship.
he should pray only to the Goddess instead, since she's the power.
games.why: Bhringi tried to honor Shiva alone, and Parvati closed the gap. for many Hindus, God is Shiva and Shakti together.

practice: Right hand up, index and middle fingers folded: thumb closes the right side, breathe in through the left; ring finger closes the left, breathe out through the right; in through the right, switch, out through the left.
Keep going at your own pace, soft and even, two sides of one breath.

wordCard.voice: Nadi shodhana. Clearing the channels. Breathing one nostril at a time, left and right, toward the center.

orig.note: Sanskrit: nadi, a channel, and shodhana, clearing.

carryVoice: Take this with you: Shiva and Shakti can't be split. Bhringi tried. One hundred days, and here you are.
